justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 91.8 for the one-day forecast and rising slightly to 93.0 at one month. This pattern suggests I was working from a baseline assumption of mild positive momentum, likely anchored to a recent price or index level with a small expected return baked in — consistent with long-run equity drift or a slightly bullish near-term signal. The one-day estimate is tightly anchored to the current observed value because little new information typically arrives overnight, while the weekly and monthly estimates incorporate a small positive drift premium reflecting the general tendency of risk assets to trend upward over moderate horizons when no specific bearish catalyst is identified.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the time horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 6.6 units, capturing normal intraday-to-next-day volatility. By one week, it has widened to 15 units, and by one month to 28 units, reflecting the accumulation of unpredictable news, macro data releases, and market sentiment shifts. These widths were likely calibrated against historical volatility — implying an annualized volatility somewhere in the range of 15–25%, which is typical for broad equity indices or moderately volatile individual assets.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing earnings or economic data release — could quickly breach the lower bound, especially at the one-week and one-month horizons. Liquidity events or contagion from correlated markets could amplify moves beyond what historical volatility would suggest. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as a major policy stimulus announcement, better-than-expected economic data, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical risk could push the asset above the upper bound.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly log-normal return distributions, which tend to underweight the probability of fat-tailed events. Real financial markets exhibit excess kurtosis, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution implies. Any period of elevated systemic stress — a credit event, a flash crash, or a sudden shift in correlation regimes — would likely invalidate the stated intervals regardless of horizon. Treating the 90% confidence interval as a hard boundary would be a mistake; it is better understood as a central tendency range that captures most routine variation but not all plausible outcomes.
